clue.text: School fag's pronouncement

indicators.note: a pronouncement is something spoken, so the cigarette brand is to be heard rather than read

parts.note: fag is British slang for a cigarette, and Marlboro is a well-known cigarette brand

explanation.surface: A junior boy at a public school, the fag, makes an announcement.
explanation.walkthrough: At English public schools a fag was a junior who ran errands for seniors, which is the misdirection; here a fag is a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: Marlborough College is an English public school in Wiltshire.

clue.text: Movement of infantry in frontier area

explanation.surface: Foot soldiers advance through border country.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers move in step on a route-walk; separately, the marches are border districts, as between England and Wales.

clue.text: Put up Gregory's middle name

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up means writing it upwards, so the letters run backwards
the middle signals dropping the first and last letters of Gregory and keeping the rest

explanation.surface: Someone nominates the middle name of a man called Gregory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle' takes REGOR from Gregory (all but its first and last letters); 'Put up' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger is a common male given name.

clue.text: Busy changing deliveries for bribes

indicators.note: changing tells us the letters of the word busy are rearranged

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six deliveries from one bowler

explanation.surface: A busy courier switches deliveries in exchange for bribes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing' rearranges BUSY into BUYS. An over is a set of six balls bowled in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: To win someone round with payment is to corrupt them with inducements, the same as bribing them.

clue.text: Staff and head of Eton were on high horse, perhaps

parts.note: a staff is a stick or rod

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only the opening letter of Eton is taken

explanation.surface: Teachers and the headmaster of Eton were arrogant, on their high horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On one's high horse' means haughty; here it is taken literally, sitting on a tall animal. ETON is an English public school.
explanation.definitionFit: Being seated on a mount and travelling is past-tense riding.

clue.text: University recently admitting boy, after all

indicators.note: admitting means letting something in, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: recently means lately
Tim is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A university has recently taken in a boy after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'after all' as 'boy, after all'; it is the definition, meaning eventually.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean in the end, eventually, when everything is considered.

clue.text: Announced German composer's name

indicators.note: announced means spoken out, so the composer's surname is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: George Frideric Handel was a German-born composer

explanation.surface: The name of a German composer was announced.
explanation.definitionFit: A handle is slang for a person's name or nickname.

clue.text: Make mistakes in English -reading and writing, perhaps?

parts.note: reading is one of the three Rs of basic schooling
writing is another of the three Rs

explanation.surface: Pupils slip up in English, in reading and writing.
explanation.walkthrough: The three Rs are reading, (w)riting and (a)rithmetic, so each counts as an R.
explanation.definitionFit: To blunder or go wrong is to commit errors.

clue.text: Be holding 25 wrongly, as fanatic

indicators.note: holding means containing, so one word is placed inside the other

parts.note: to be is to exist

indicators.note: wrongly tells us the letters of the cross-referenced word are put in a different order

parts.note: 25 refers to the answer at 25-down, the word for a school period

explanation.surface: Someone holds a view of a school period wrongly and becomes a fanatic.
explanation.walkthrough: 25-down is the answer to that clue, a school period; 'wrongly' scrambles it before 'holding' encloses it.
explanation.definitionFit: A zealot holding immoderate views is called an extremist.

clue.text: Plan again to introduce new standard for sailors

indicators.note: to introduce something is to bring it in, so a letter is put inside the other word

parts.note: to plan again is to redesign

explanation.surface: Designers plan afresh to bring in a new flag for the navy.
explanation.walkthrough: A standard is a flag; the Red Ensign is the flag flown by British merchant ships.
explanation.definitionFit: The red ensign is the flag of the British merchant navy, a banner for seamen.

clue.text: Something precious divided by good sport

indicators.note: divided by means split, so another letter sits inside the word

parts.note: a ruby is a precious stone

explanation.surface: A precious item gets split by a decent fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good sport' looks like a phrase for a pleasant person; it splits into G and the definition. Rugby is also an English public school.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby is a football game played with an oval ball.

clue.text: Set off from school in old hat

indicators.note: in shows one word goes inside the other

parts.note: old hat means out of date, dated
Eton College is an English public school

explanation.surface: A pupil leaves school wearing an old hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old hat' looks like headgear but means outmoded.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off a bomb is to explode it.

clue.text: Hard weapon producing distress

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
an arrow is a weapon

explanation.surface: A tough weapon causes suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: Harrow is also an English public school.
explanation.definitionFit: To harrow is to torment or upset deeply, as in a harrowing experience.

clue.text: For French, bad novelist not quite in old school

parts.note: mal is French for bad

indicators.note: not quite means the word falls short by its final letter

parts.note: Jules Verne was a French novelist

explanation.surface: A poor French novelist is not quite fitting into an old school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' drops the last letter of VERNE.
explanation.definitionFit: Malvern College is a long-established English public school in Worcestershire.

clue.text: Overthrow of monarchs? Not us!

parts.note: the clue plays on a mock split into 'for' plus 'reigners', as if a word for those against rulers, while 'Not us!' gives the plain sense of outsiders, people of other nations

explanation.surface: Someone denies having any part in overthrowing kings.
explanation.definitionFit: People from abroad are those who are not one of us, outsiders from other countries.

clue.text: Catholic college putting liberal out

parts.note: liberal can mean generous, plentiful, ample
forth means out, as in go forth

explanation.surface: A Catholic college is turning out liberals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'liberal' looks political but means generous. Ampleforth is a Benedictine Catholic school in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Ampleforth College is a Roman Catholic boarding school run by Benedictine monks.

clue.text: Conservative old boy included in top honours, such as these

indicators.note: included in means placed inside, so these letters go within the other word

parts.note: aces means top-class, the best
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A Conservative old boy receives top honours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'included in' puts COLAD inside ACES.
explanation.definitionFit: Accolades are marks of praise or awards bestowed on someone.

clue.text: One chap I repeatedly upset in the old country

indicators.note: upset means overturned, so the letters are rearranged
repeatedly means the letter I is used twice

explanation.surface: A man keeps getting upset about the old country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repeatedly' doubles I; 'upset' rearranges ONE, CHAP and II.
explanation.definitionFit: Phoenicia was an ancient land on the eastern Mediterranean coast.

clue.text: Fruit person found in 19, for example

definitions.meaning: a small brown hairy fruit with green flesh
19 is the capital of New Zealand, so this is a New Zealander, nicknamed after the national bird

explanation.surface: Fruit may come from a person in a particular city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chinese gooseberry is called by this name, and so, informally, is any New Zealander.

clue.text: Where cup is, of course, for support

definitions.meaning: on a golf course the cup is the hole, which sits beneath the flagstick
to support from below, to shore up

explanation.surface: Where the trophy sits, naturally, as support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally' but means on a golf course; the pin is the flagstick.
explanation.definitionFit: The golf hole lies beneath the flag; and to brace a structure from below is to buttress it.

clue.text: Dunce in class on sacred books

parts.note: CL is an abbreviation for class
OT, the Old Testament, is a set of sacred books

explanation.surface: The dunce in class sits on the holy books.
explanation.definitionFit: A clot is British slang for a stupid person.

clue.text: Wife meeting one duke or another

parts.note: Duke Ellington was a jazz bandleader

explanation.surface: A wife meets one duke or another.
explanation.walkthrough: One duke is the jazzman Duke Ellington; 'another' is the Duke of Wellington. Wellington College is also an English school.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Wellesley, victor of Waterloo, was made Duke of Wellington, a second duke besides the jazzman.

clue.text: Bat poorly, getting duck — wickets falling at both ends

parts.note: W is the cricket abbreviation for wickets
poorly means ill
a duck, a score of zero in cricket, looks like O
the same abbreviation again, the clue says the wickets fall at both ends

explanation.surface: A batsman plays badly, is out for a duck, and wickets tumble at each end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at both ends' puts a W either side of ILL and O. Cricket bats are made of willow.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket bats are made from the timber of a tree of this name.

clue.text: Opening in theatre, with releasing effect

definitions.meaning: cutting open in an operating theatre
piercing a boil releases its contents

explanation.surface: An opening night in a theatre has a liberating effect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Theatre' means an operating theatre, not a playhouse. Lancing College is an English school in Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon pierces an abscess with a lancet, letting the pus out.

clue.text: Scottish school's galas needing extra time

indicators.note: needing an extra letter means one is added inside the word

parts.note: fetes are galas or festivals

explanation.surface: A Scottish school's galas run into extra time.
explanation.walkthrough: Fettes College is a public school in Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: Fettes College is an independent boarding school in Edinburgh.

clue.text: Left-winger collects a card

indicators.note: collects means gathers in, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: Trot is short for Trotskyist, a left-winger

explanation.surface: A socialist collects a card.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarot is one of a pack of cards used in fortune-telling.

clue.text: Box, in practice, containing European missile

indicators.note: containing means holding inside, so the letter goes within the word

parts.note: to spar is to box for practice

explanation.surface: A practice box contains a European missile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a container but is boxing.
explanation.definitionFit: A spear is a thrown weapon, a missile.

clue.text: Schooldays in Winchester, maybe

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the run of letters across the words Winchester and maybe

explanation.surface: Someone recalls school days at Winchester, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Winchester College is an English public school, so the clue reads as a whole-clue description; in fact the letters straddle 'Winchester' and 'maybe'.
explanation.definitionFit: A school period of several weeks of classes is a single block of schooldays.

clue.text: Revealing, in upfront fashion

parts.note: describes a style of dress with a low neckline that shows the chest, 'upfront' being literal

explanation.surface: Someone is being frank and open about something.
explanation.definitionFit: A décolleté dress has a low-cut neckline exposing the neck and shoulders.

clue.text: Intrinsically, in proper sense

definitions.meaning: by its very nature, in itself
strictly speaking, in the precise meaning

explanation.surface: Something is essentially, strictly speaking, so.
explanation.walkthrough: The Perse is also a school in Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means by or in itself, so as such or strictly considered.

clue.text: Resort that's in Belgium, not in Spain

indicators.note: not means the following word is left out

explanation.surface: A resort is in Belgium, not Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not in' removes IN from SPAIN. Spa in Belgium gave its name to all spas.
explanation.definitionFit: Spa is a Belgian town famed for its mineral springs.

clue.text: Point by member of government abandoning one parliamentary position

parts.note: west is a compass point

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving out a letter from the word

parts.note: a minister is a member of the government
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A government minister gives up a parliamentary seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoning one' drops I from MINISTER. Westminster is where Parliament sits, and Westminster School is a London school.
explanation.definitionFit: Westminster is the London district housing the Houses of Parliament.
